idiom_name: non-overridable skeleton operation calling primitive operations and hook operations
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: write the algorithm once as a concrete operation of an abstract base class and make that operation non-overridable (the language's default for non-virtual members, or an explicit final/sealed/closed marker). Each varying step becomes its own operation on the same class: declare the required ones abstract so implementations must provide them, and give the optional ones a default body - often empty - so subclasses may override them. The skeleton calls the steps in a fixed order and may also call shared concrete operations and factory methods; subclasses never restate the skeleton. Document which steps are required and which are optional, and keep the base class from calling its own published operations so a subclass cannot bypass the invariant. In Python, use abc.ABC with @abstractmethod for required steps, a standard method with a pass or ellipsis body for hooks, and @final from typing for static-analysis enforcement of the non-overridable skeleton.
code_sketch:
abstract class Algorithm:                 # skeleton in the base class
    def run(self, input):                 # must not be overridden
        prepared = self.prepare(input)    # required primitive operation
        self.trace(prepared)              # hook: default no-op
        return self.finish(prepared)      # required primitive operation
# subclass implements prepare() and finish(); it inherits run() unchanged
pitfalls: Leaving the skeleton overridable so that one subclass replaces the whole algorithm — the invariant the pattern exists to protect is then gone.
Mixing required and optional steps without documenting which is which, so subclass authors override the wrong members or skip a step the algorithm depends on.
Growing the base class into a configuration kit: every conceivable extension point becomes a hook and subclasses end up implementing a large fraction of the algorithm.
Calling the steps from the constructor or from other published operations, so they run before the subclass is initialised or run twice.
Making step methods public so external clients bypass the template method and call steps directly, breaking the guaranteed sequence.
Deep inheritance hierarchies: more than one intermediate abstract layer means a second variation axis has crept in — refactor to composition or extract a second pattern.
Allowing steps to throw checked exceptions the template method does not declare, silently breaking callers that expect a clean contract.
Adding side effects to the skeleton method itself (logging, timing, validation) instead of delegating to named hook points, making the skeleton harder to reason about.
Returning value from primitive operations that the template method ignores in some concrete variants — signals the step interface is wrong and the template method may be doing too much.

Wrong move: rename, split or reorder a step in the base class because the compiler only checks signatures -> failure: subclasses silently keep the old override of a now-dead member or inherit the new default and skip work the skeleton assumed, so the invariant breaks in production instead of at compile time -> instead: treat the step set as versioned API - deprecate the old step, keep it delegating to the new one for a migration period, and assert the step order with a recording subclass.

Wrong move: enforce a must-run-before/must-run-after rule inside an overridable hook because the skeleton is already final -> failure: a subclass that overrides the hook without calling super drops the guard, and every other variant silently loses the protection -> instead: keep guards in the non-overridable skeleton itself, or if the language cannot make it final, apply the non-virtual interface idiom: a final public wrapper that runs the invariant and then calls the protected hook.

Wrong move: let steps communicate through mutable fields on the base class -> failure: step N's half-written state leaks into step M, hooks observe values the author never set, and a subclass cannot reuse the steps out of order or in parallel -> instead: pass step results forward as parameters/return values through the skeleton and keep base-class state immutable or thread-confined.
